{{for multi|the computer networking term|Hyperconnectivity|hyper-connectivity in node-link graphs|Connectivity (graph theory)#Super- and hyper-connectivity}}

In the mathematical field of [[topology]], a '''hyperconnected space'''<ref>Steen & Seebach, p. 29</ref>{{sfn|Hart|Nagata|Vaughan|2004|p=9}} or '''irreducible space'''{{sfn|Hart|Nagata|Vaughan|2004|p=9}} is a [[topological space]] ''X'' that cannot be written as the union of two proper closed subsets (whether disjoint or non-disjoint). The name ''irreducible space'' is preferred in [[algebraic geometry]].

For a topological space ''X'' the following conditions are equivalent:
* No two nonempty [[open set]]s are [[disjoint sets|disjoint]].
* ''X'' cannot be written as the union of two proper [[closed subset]]s.
* Every nonempty open set is [[dense (topology)|dense]] in ''X''.
* Every open set is connected.
* The [[interior (topology)|interior]] of every proper closed subset of ''X'' is empty.
* Every subset is dense or [[Nowhere dense set|nowhere dense]] in ''X''.
* No two points can be separated by disjoint neighbourhoods.

A space which satisfies any one of these conditions is called ''hyperconnected'' or ''irreducible''.  Due to the condition about neighborhoods of distinct points being in a sense the opposite of the [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] property, some authors call such spaces '''anti-Hausdorff'''.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1016/0166-8641(93)90147-6|title = An anti-Hausdorff Fréchet space in which convergent sequences have unique limits|year = 1993|last1 = Van Douwen|first1 = Eric K.|journal = Topology and Its Applications|volume = 51|issue = 2|pages = 147–158|doi-access = free}}</ref>

The [[empty set]] is [[vacuous truth|vacuously]] a hyperconnected or irreducible space under the definition above (because it contains no nonempty open sets).  However some authors,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/004U|title = Section 5.8 (004U): Irreducible components—The Stacks project}}</ref> especially those interested in applications to [[algebraic geometry]], add an explicit condition that an irreducible space must be nonempty. 

An '''irreducible set''' is a subset of a topological space for which the [[subspace topology]] is irreducible.

== Examples ==
Two examples of hyperconnected spaces from [[point set topology]] are the [[cofinite topology]] on any [[infinite set]] and the [[Order topology#Left and right order topologies|right order topology]] on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>.

In algebraic geometry, taking the [[spectrum of a ring]] whose [[reduced ring]] is an [[integral domain]] is an irreducible topological space—applying the [[lattice theorem]] to the [[nilradical of a ring|nilradical]], which is within every prime, to show the spectrum of the quotient map is a [[homeomorphism]], this reduces to the irreducibility of the spectrum of an integral domain. For example, the [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]]s<blockquote><math>\text{Spec}\left( \frac{\mathbb{Z}[x,y,z]}{x^4 + y^3 + z^2} \right)</math> , <math>\text{Proj}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]}{(y^2z - x(x-z)(x-2z))} \right)</math></blockquote>are irreducible since in both cases the polynomials defining the ideal are irreducible polynomials (meaning they have no non-trivial factorization). A non-example is given by the [[normal crossing divisor]]<blockquote><math>\text{Spec}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]}{(xyz)} \right)</math></blockquote>since the underlying space is the union of the affine planes <math>\mathbb{A}^2_{x,y}</math>, <math>\mathbb{A}^2_{x,z}</math>, and <math>\mathbb{A}^2_{y,z}</math>. Another non-example is given by the scheme<blockquote><math>\text{Proj}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,w]}{(xy, f_4)} \right)</math></blockquote>where <math>f_4</math> is an irreducible degree 4 [[homogeneous polynomial]]. This is the union of the two genus 3 curves (by the [[genus–degree formula]])<blockquote><math>\text{Proj}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[y,z,w]}{(f_4(0,y,z,w))} \right), \text{ } \text{Proj}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x,z,w]}{(f_4(x,0,z,w))} \right)</math></blockquote>

== Hyperconnectedness vs. connectedness ==
Every hyperconnected space is both [[connected space|connected]] and [[locally connected]] (though not necessarily [[path-connected]] or [[locally path-connected]]). 

Note that in the definition of hyper-connectedness, the closed sets need not be disjoint. This is in contrast to the definition of connectedness, in which the open sets are disjoint.

For example, the space of real numbers with the standard topology is connected but ''not'' hyperconnected. This is because it cannot be written as the union of two disjoint open sets, but it ''can'' be written as the union of two (non-disjoint) closed sets.

== Properties ==
*The nonempty open subsets of a hyperconnected space are "large" in the sense that each one is dense in ''X'' and any pair of them intersects. Thus, a hyperconnected space cannot be [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] if it contains more than one point.
*Every hyperconnected space is both [[connected space|connected]] and [[locally connected]] (though not necessarily [[path-connected]] or [[locally path-connected]]).
*Since the closure of every non-empty open set in a hyperconnected space is the whole space, which is an open set, every hyperconnected space is [[extremally disconnected space|extremally disconnected]].
*The image of a hyperconnected space under a [[continuous function (topology)|continuous function]] is hyperconnected.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Commutative Algebra: Chapters 1-7|last=Bourbaki|first=Nicolas|author-link=Nicolas Bourbaki|publisher=Springer|year=1989|isbn=978-3-540-64239-8|pages=95}}</ref> In particular, any continuous function from a hyperconnected space to a Hausdorff space must be constant. It follows that every hyperconnected space is [[pseudocompact space|pseudocompact]].
*Every open subspace of a hyperconnected space is hyperconnected.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Commutative Algebra: Chapters 1-7|last=Bourbaki|first=Nicolas|publisher=Springer|year=1989|isbn=978-3-540-64239-8|pages=95}}</ref>
: Proof: ''Let <math>U\subset X</math> be an open subset. Any two disjoint open subsets of <math>U</math> would themselves be disjoint open subsets of <math>X</math>.  So at least one of them must be empty.''
* More generally, every dense subset of a hyperconnected space is hyperconnected.
: Proof: ''Suppose <math>S</math> is a dense subset of <math>X</math> and <math>S=S_1\cup S_2</math> with <math>S_1</math>, <math>S_2</math> closed in <math>S</math>.  Then <math>X=\overline S=\overline{S_1}\cup\overline{S_2}</math>.  Since <math>X</math> is hyperconnected, one of the two closures is the whole space <math>X</math>, say <math>\overline{S_1}=X</math>.  This implies that <math>S_1</math> is dense in <math>S</math>, and since it is closed in <math>S</math>, it must be equal to <math>S</math>.''
*A closed subspace of a hyperconnected space need not be hyperconnected.
: Counterexample: ''<math>\Bbbk^2</math> with <math>\Bbbk</math> an [[algebraically closed field]] (thus infinite) is hyperconnected<ref>{{Cite book|title=Algebraic Geometry. An introduction|last=Perrin|first=Daniel|publisher=Springer|year=2008|isbn=978-1-84800-055-1|pages=14}}</ref> in the [[Zariski topology]], while <math>V=Z(XY)=Z(X)\cup Z(Y)\subset\Bbbk^2</math> is closed and not hyperconnected.''
*The [[closure (topology)|closure]] of any irreducible set is irreducible.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/004W|title = Lemma 5.8.3 (004W)—The Stacks project}}</ref>
: Proof: ''Suppose <math>S\subseteq X</math> where <math>S</math> is irreducible and write <math>\operatorname{Cl}_X(S)=F\cup G</math> for two closed subsets <math>F,G\subseteq \operatorname{Cl}_X(S)</math> (and thus in <math>X</math>). <math>F':=F\cap S,\,G':=G\cap S</math> are closed in <math>S</math> and <math>S=F'\cup G'</math> which implies <math>S\subseteq F</math> or <math>S\subseteq G</math>, but then <math>\operatorname{Cl}_X(S)=F</math> or <math>\operatorname{Cl}_X(S)=G</math> by definition of [[closure (topology)|closure]].''
*A space <math>X</math> which can be written as <math>X=U_1\cup U_2</math> with <math>U_1,U_2\subset X</math> open and irreducible such that <math>U_1\cap U_2\ne\emptyset</math> is irreducible.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Commutative Algebra: Chapters 1-7|last=Bourbaki|first=Nicolas|publisher=Springer|year=1989|isbn=978-3-540-64239-8|pages=95}}</ref>
: Proof: ''Firstly, we notice that if <math>V</math> is a non-empty open set in <math>X</math> then it intersects both <math>U_1</math> and <math>U_2</math>; indeed, suppose <math>V_1:=U_1\cap V\ne\emptyset</math>, then <math>V_1</math> is dense in <math>U_1</math>, thus <math>\exists x\in\operatorname{Cl}_{U_1}(V_1)\cap U_2=U_1\cap U_2\ne\emptyset</math> and <math>x\in U_2</math> is a [[point of closure]] of <math>V_1</math> which implies <math>V_1\cap U_2\ne\emptyset</math> and a fortiori <math>V_2:=V\cap U_2\ne\emptyset</math>. Now <math>V=V\cap(U_1\cup U_2)=V_1\cup V_2</math> and taking the closure <math>\operatorname{Cl}_{X}(V)\supseteq{\operatorname{Cl}}_{U_1}(V_1)\cup{\operatorname{Cl}}_{U_2}(V_2)=U_1\cup U_2=X,</math> therefore <math>V</math> is a non-empty open and dense subset of <math>X</math>. Since this is true for every non-empty open subset, <math>X</math> is irreducible.''

==Irreducible components==

An '''[[irreducible component]]'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/004V|title = Definition 5.8.1 (004V)—The Stacks project}}</ref> in a topological space is a maximal irreducible subset (i.e. an irreducible set that is not contained in any larger irreducible set). The irreducible components are always closed.

Every irreducible subset of a space ''X'' is contained in a (not necessarily unique) irreducible component of ''X''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/004W|title = Lemma 5.8.3 (004W)—The Stacks project}}</ref>  In particular, every point of ''X'' is contained in some irreducible component of ''X''.  Unlike the [[connected component (topology)|connected component]]s of a space, the irreducible components need not be disjoint (i.e. they need not form a [[partition of a set|partition]]). In general, the irreducible components will overlap.

The irreducible components of a Hausdorff space are just the [[singleton set]]s.

Since every irreducible space is connected, the irreducible components will always lie in the connected components.

Every [[Noetherian topological space]] has finitely many irreducible components.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0050|title = Section 5.9 (0050): Noetherian topological spaces—The Stacks project}}</ref>
